Event logs and interoperability

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/event-logs.Rmd
event-logs.Rmd

Lag sequential analysis counts transitions between consecutive events of the same sequence. What counts as a sequence therefore decides what counts as a transition: two actions by different students are not a transition, and neither are the last action of one working session and the first action of the next one a day later. With data that arrive as an event log, one row per recorded action, the analysis starts by recovering the sequences: which rows belong together, in what order, and where a sequence ends.

lsa() performs that step itself. It accepts wide sequence data, a long event log described by a small set of column arguments, and the sequence objects of the tna and Nestimate packages, and it returns a fit whose transition probabilities, initial probabilities, and network can be handed back to those packages. This guide covers each input form, the rules that split a log into sequences, grouped logs, and the export of a fit. The column grammar is the one used by tna::prepare_data() and Nestimate::build_network(), so a log prepared for one of them needs no change.

library(lagdynamics)

Data

Three bundled data sets cover the input forms.

  • group_regulation_long: an event log of collaborative learning, 27,533 rows. Actor: Actor (2,000 students). Action: Action, nine regulation codes. Time: Time, a POSIXct time stamp. Group: Achiever (High or Low), fixed for each actor.
  • ai_long: an event log of coded AI behaviours in human-AI programming sessions, 8,551 rows. Actor: project (34 projects). Session: session_id (428 sessions). Action: code, eight behaviour codes. Order: order_in_session, the position of the coded message within its session.
  • group_regulation and engagement: wide data, one row per sequence and one column per time point.
head(group_regulation_long)

head(ai_long)

#> 2       3441 Project_7 0086cabebd15 1772661600   2026-03-05        Plan  Repair

Wide sequence data

Wide data need no column arguments: each row is a sequence and the columns are read in order. group_regulation holds the same 2,000 sequences as the long log above, already assembled.

fit_wide <- lsa(group_regulation)
as.data.frame(summary(fit_wide))
#>      engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha  lrx2
#> 1 classical   1        9        2000    27533         25533            72  0.05 13204
#>   lrx2_df lrx2_p    x2 x2_df x2_p
#> 1      64      0 15435    64    0

The wide data give 2,000 sequences with 25,533 transitions among nine states. Sequences differ in length, and the missing cells that pad the shorter rows are dropped, so no transition is counted into or out of them.

Long event logs

A long log is described by naming its columns, as strings:

Argument Role
action The state of each event. Required; naming it switches to long-format input.
actor Who produced the event. Each actor’s events form a sequence.
session A working session. Each session, or each actor-session pair when both are given, forms a sequence.
time A time stamp that orders the events (POSIXct, a parseable string, or Unix time with is_unix_time = TRUE).
order An explicit position that orders the events; used in preference to time.
group A grouping column, fixed within each sequence, for one model per group.

The regulation log has an actor, an action, and a time stamp.

fit_long <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                time = "Time")
as.data.frame(summary(fit_long))
#>      engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha  lrx2
#> 1 classical   1        9        2000    27533         25533            72  0.05 13204
#>   lrx2_df lrx2_p    x2 x2_df x2_p
#> 1      64      0 15435    64    0

The log is assembled into 2,000 sequences, one per actor, with the same 25,533 transitions as the wide data. The two fits are the same model:

isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_long), transitions(fit_wide),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
#> [1] TRUE

Where a sequence ends

When time is given without session, a sequence also ends wherever two consecutive events of an actor are more than time_threshold seconds apart, 900 seconds (15 minutes) by default. The threshold is an analytic choice: it states how long a pause has to be before the next action no longer counts as a response to the previous one. A shorter threshold splits the same log into more, shorter sequences.

fit_5min <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                time = "Time", time_threshold = 300)
as.data.frame(summary(fit_5min))
#>      engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha lrx2
#> 1 classical   1        9       12305    27533         15228            69  0.05 7927
#>   lrx2_df lrx2_p   x2 x2_df x2_p
#> 1      64      0 9222    64    0

With a five-minute threshold the 2,000 actor logs break into 12,305 sequences, and the number of transitions falls from 25,533 to 15,228: every pause longer than five minutes removes the transition that spanned it. The independence test remains decisive (G² = 7,927 on 64 degrees of freedom) and 69 transitions stay significant, against 72 with the default, so the structure of the process does not hinge on the threshold. Comparing the fit at two thresholds in this way is the sensitivity check the choice needs.

Without actor or session, the whole log is one stream ordered by time. The regulation log interleaves 2,000 students working at the same time, so a single stream mixes their actions into transitions that never happened:

fit_stream <- lsa(group_regulation_long, action = "Action", time = "Time")
as.data.frame(summary(fit_stream))
#>      engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha lrx2
#> 1 classical   1        9           1    27533         27532             1  0.05 46.2
#>   lrx2_df lrx2_p x2 x2_df  x2_p
#> 1      64  0.954 46    64 0.957

The stream gives one sequence of 27,532 transitions, and its independence test is not significant (G² = 46.2, df = 64, p = 0.954): interleaving the students destroys the sequential structure. The actor argument is what makes the regulation log analysable.

Sessions and explicit order

The AI log records sessions within projects and an explicit position of each coded message within its session. Naming actor and session makes each project-session pair a sequence, and order sets the order of events within it. Several codes can share a message, and the position column keeps them in the order they were coded.

fit_ai <- lsa(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
              action = "code", order = "order_in_session")
fit_ai
#> Lag Sequential Analysis  -  classical  (lag 1, directed)
#>   8 states | 8123 transitions | 8551 events | 428 sequences
#>   states: Ask, Delegate, Execute, Explain, Investigate, Plan, Repair, Report
#>   independence: G² = 2168.1, df = 49, p <2e-16
#> 
#>   Significant transitions (p < 0.05): 40 of 64
#>   strongest over-represented (of 19):
#>     Investigate -> Plan  z =  +33.4  ***
#>     Delegate -> Plan     z =  +18.1  ***
#>     Ask -> Explain       z =  +16.4  ***
#>     Execute -> Execute   z =  +16.1  ***
#>     Explain -> Report    z =  +14.0  ***
#>     ... and 14 more
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     Investigate 0.715  ████████████████████████
#>     Delegate    0.185  ██████
#>     Execute     0.058  ██
#>     Plan        0.035  █
#>     Ask         0.005  
#>     Explain     0.002  
#>     Repair      0.000  
#>     Report      0.000

The log yields 428 sequences, one per session, with 8,123 transitions among eight codes. Forty of the 64 transitions depart from chance, and the strongest favoured transition is Investigate -> Plan (z = 33.4). Most sessions open with Investigate (initial probability 0.715).

Large logs: the actor-session key

When both actor and session are given, the sequence key is built over the full cross of distinct actors and distinct sessions. The size of that cross is held in an R integer, so once the number of distinct actors times the number of distinct sessions passes 2,147,483,647, the largest integer R can hold, the key overflows. The affected events lose their sequence and are dropped, and the only sign is an “NAs produced by integer overflow” warning. A log of 50,000 actors and 50,000 sessions is enough to trigger it.

On a large log, compare the number of sequences in the summary with the number of distinct sessions. When the session identifiers are already unique across actors, as in ai_long, pass the session column as actor and omit session; the key is then built over the sessions alone.

fit_ai_sessions <- lsa(ai_long, actor = "session_id", action = "code",
                       order = "order_in_session")
as.data.frame(summary(fit_ai_sessions))
#>      engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha lrx2
#> 1 classical   1        8         428     8551          8123            40  0.05 2168
#>   lrx2_df lrx2_p   x2 x2_df x2_p
#> 1      49      0 2485    49    0
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_ai_sessions), transitions(fit_ai),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
#> [1] TRUE

Keying on the session alone recovers the same 428 sequences and an identical transition table, so the two calls are interchangeable here, and only the second one is safe on a log too large for the cross.

Grouped long logs

Adding group fits one model per group from the same log, under one shared set of states. The grouping column must take a single value within each recovered sequence; a sequence that spans two groups is an error.

gfit <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
            time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
gfit
#> <lsa_group>
#>   engine:    classical
#>   states:    9 (adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan, synthesis)
#>   groups:    2
#>     - High:        1000 sequences
#>     - Low:         1000 sequences
summary(gfit)
#>   group    engine lag n_states n_sequences n_events n_transitions n_significant alpha
#> 1  High classical   1        9        1000    13721         12721            66  0.05
#> 2   Low classical   1        9        1000    13812         12812            67  0.05
#>   lrx2 lrx2_df lrx2_p   x2 x2_df x2_p
#> 1 6147      64      0 6807    64    0
#> 2 7715      64      0 9197    64    0

The high and the low achievers contribute 1,000 sequences each, with 12,721 and 12,812 transitions. Every reading verb on a grouped fit returns a leading group column, and the grouped fit is the input of the group comparisons covered in the group-comparison vignette.

transitions(gfit, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(4)
#>   group      from        to lag count expected   prob prob_col adj_res         p yules_q
#> 1  High   emotion  cohesion   1   505    114.0 0.3258  0.53953    40.6  0.00e+00   0.847
#> 2  High consensus consensus   1   283    917.0 0.0834  0.08229   -28.6 3.68e-180  -0.698
#> 3  High   discuss synthesis   1   213     46.1 0.1063  0.72696    27.1 1.79e-161   0.881
#> 4  High   discuss      plan   1    25    458.8 0.0125  0.00858   -25.1 2.35e-139  -0.934
#>    kappa kappa_z   kappa_p   lift  sign significant
#> 1  0.425    37.7 6.36e-311 4.4280  over        TRUE
#> 2 -0.709   -30.1 5.36e-199 0.3086 under        TRUE
#> 3  0.613    25.5 5.39e-143 4.6169  over        TRUE
#> 4 -0.949   -26.0 3.81e-149 0.0545 under        TRUE

tna objects

A tna model keeps the sequences it was fitted from, and lsa() reads them directly. The model below is fitted by tna to the wide engagement data and passed to lsa().

tna_fit <- tna::tna(engagement)
tna_fit
#> State Labels : 
#> 
#>    Active, Average, Disengaged 
#> 
#> Transition Probability Matrix :
#> 
#>            Active Average Disengaged
#> Active      0.698   0.267      0.035
#> Average     0.204   0.610      0.186
#> Disengaged  0.120   0.397      0.483
#> 
#> Initial Probabilities : 
#> 
#>     Active    Average Disengaged 
#>      0.382      0.368      0.250
fit_from_tna <- lsa(tna_fit)
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_from_tna), transitions(lsa(engagement)),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
#> [1] TRUE

Loading tna prints a notice that it registers its own plot method for bootstrap results in place of the one from cograph; the notice does not concern the models. The fit from the tna model and the fit from the original data are identical. The same holds for the output of tna::prepare_data(), which lsa() accepts as it stands. A grouped tna model (group_tna) is read as well, but its groups are pooled into a single fit; for one model per group, fit the log with group = as in the previous section.

Nestimate objects

Nestimate::build_network() uses the same long-log grammar and keeps the prepared sequences in the network object, which lsa() reads.

net <- Nestimate::build_network(ai_long, method = "tna", actor = "project",
                                session = "session_id", action = "code",
                                order = "order_in_session")
#> Metadata aggregated per session: ties resolved by first occurrence in 'session_date' (4 sessions), 'cluster' (22 sessions)
fit_from_nestimate <- lsa(net)
isTRUE(all.equal(transitions(fit_from_nestimate), transitions(fit_ai),
                 check.attributes = FALSE))
#> [1] TRUE

Nestimate reports that two metadata columns (session_date and cluster) vary within some sessions and keeps their first value; the message concerns those columns only, not the sequences. The Nestimate network and the direct lsa() call on the log recover the same transition table.

From a fit to tna and other tools

A fit exposes the quantities that transition network tools consume. transition_probabilities() returns the row-stochastic transition matrix as a tidy data frame, one row per from -> to pair, and initial() the distribution of first states.

transition_probabilities(fit_long) |> head(9)
#>    from         to   prob
#> 1 adapt      adapt 0.0000
#> 2 adapt   cohesion 0.2731
#> 3 adapt  consensus 0.4774
#> 4 adapt coregulate 0.0216
#> 5 adapt    discuss 0.0589
#> 6 adapt    emotion 0.1198
#> 7 adapt    monitor 0.0334
#> 8 adapt       plan 0.0157
#> 9 adapt  synthesis 0.0000
initial(fit_long)
#>        state init_prob
#> 1      adapt    0.0115
#> 2   cohesion    0.0605
#> 3  consensus    0.2140
#> 4 coregulate    0.0190
#> 5    discuss    0.1755
#> 6    emotion    0.1515
#> 7    monitor    0.1440
#> 8       plan    0.2045
#> 9  synthesis    0.0195

The nine rows shown are the transitions out of adapt; their probabilities sum to one. The most common first states are consensus (0.2140) and plan (0.2045). For a grouped fit both tables carry a leading group column.

lsa_to_tna() converts a fit to a tna model, so the tna toolkit (centralities, communities, cliques, its plots) applies to a model estimated here. weights chooses the edge weights; "prob" gives the transition probabilities of a standard transition network.

tn <- lsa_to_tna(fit_from_tna, weights = "prob")
tna::centralities(tn, measures = c("InStrength", "OutStrength", "Betweenness"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   state      InStrength OutStrength Betweenness
#> * <fct>           <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 Active          0.324       0.302           0
#> 2 Average         0.664       0.390           2
#> 3 Disengaged      0.221       0.517           0

Average receives the most probability from the other states (in-strength 0.664) and is the only state that lies on shortest paths between the other two (betweenness 2, against 0 for Active and Disengaged). A grouped fit converts to a group_tna model, one tna model per group:

tna::centralities(lsa_to_tna(gfit), measures = "InStrength")
#> # A tibble: 18 × 3
#>    group state      InStrength
#>  * <chr> <fct>           <dbl>
#>  1 High  adapt           0.215
#>  2 High  cohesion        0.815
#>  3 High  consensus       2.95 
#>  4 High  coregulate      0.436
#>  5 High  discuss         1.12 
#>  6 High  emotion         1.00 
#>  7 High  monitor         0.301
#>  8 High  plan            1.27 
#>  9 High  synthesis       0.167
#> 10 Low   adapt           0.452
#> 11 Low   cohesion        0.799
#> 12 Low   consensus       2.42 
#> 13 Low   coregulate      0.689
#> 14 Low   discuss         1.21 
#> 15 Low   emotion         0.808
#> 16 Low   monitor         0.393
#> 17 Low   plan            1.15 
#> 18 Low   synthesis       0.216

consensus is the state with the most incoming probability in both groups, with in-strength 2.95 among the high achievers and 2.42 among the low achievers.

A fit is also a cograph_network, so it can be drawn directly as a transition network with probability weights; the displays are covered in the plotting guide.

Summary

Input Call
Wide data, one row per sequence lsa(data)
Long log, one sequence per actor lsa(log, actor = , action = , time = )
Long log with sessions and explicit order lsa(log, actor = , session = , action = , order = )
Very large log with globally unique sessions lsa(log, actor = "<session column>", action = , order = )
One model per group add group =
tna model, tna::prepare_data() output lsa(object)
Nestimate network or prepared data lsa(object)
Hand a fit to tna lsa_to_tna(fit)
Transition and initial probabilities as tables transition_probabilities(fit), initial(fit)
